claim: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) suppresses inflammation and autoimmune diseases in preclinical and clinical studies.
source: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) suppresses inflammation and autoimmune diseases in preclinical and clinical studies.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior research.

claim: The underlying molecular, neurological, and anatomical mechanisms of VNS have been well characterized using acute electrophysiological stimulation of the vagus.
source: The underlying molecular, neurological, and anatomical mechanisms have been well characterized using acute electrophysiological stimulation of the vagus.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge in the field, supported by the literature review in the introduction.

claim: Significant heart rate responses were observed for at least 4 weeks in 60–90% of animals with the chronic VNS implant.
source: We observed significant heart rate responses for at least 4 weeks in 60–90% of animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3 showing functional implants over time.

claim: Device implantation did not impair vagus-mediated reflexes.
source: Device implantation did not impair vagus-mediated reflexes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on baroreflex, breathing reflexes, weight change, and food intake presented in Figure 4.

claim: VNS using this implant significantly suppressed TNF levels in endotoxemia.
source: VNS using this implant significantly suppressed TNF levels in endotoxemia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LPS endotoxemia experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Histological examination of implanted nerves revealed fibrotic encapsulation without axonal pathology.
source: Histological examination of implanted nerves revealed fibrotic encapsulation without axonal pathology.
evidence: This is supported by histological data and images presented in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The vagus nerve is the principal nerve of the parasympathetic nervous system.
source: The vagus nerve (VN), the principal nerve of the parasympathetic nervous system, occupies a crucial role in the reflex control of physiological homeostasis (Berthoud and Neuhuber, 2000).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation to Berthoud and Neuhuber, 2000.

claim: The vagus nerve occupies a crucial role in the reflex control of physiological homeostasis.
source: The vagus nerve (VN), the principal nerve of the parasympathetic nervous system, occupies a crucial role in the reflex control of physiological homeostasis (Berthoud and Neuhuber, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berthoud and Neuhuber, 2000.

claim: The roles of VN reflexes in controlling the cardiovascular, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal systems have been studied for more than 100 years.
source: The roles of VN reflexes in controlling the cardiovascular, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal systems have been studied for more than 100 years, but only recently has the role of VN reflexes been studied in controlling inflammation (Pavlov et al., 2020; Pavlov et al., 2018; Tracey, 2009; Tracey, 2002).
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by the context and citations provided.

claim: The role of VN reflexes in controlling inflammation has only recently been studied.
source: The roles of VN reflexes in controlling the cardiovascular, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal systems have been studied for more than 100 years, but only recently has the role of VN reflexes been studied in controlling inflammation (Pavlov et al., 2020; Pavlov et al., 2018; Tracey, 2009; Tracey, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work by Pavlov et al. and Tracey.

claim: VN mechanisms termed 'the inflammatory reflex' inhibit cytokine production in the spleen and attenuate inflammation in preclinical and clinical studies.
source: We and others have defined VN mechanisms, termed 'the inflammatory reflex (IR),' which inhibit cytokine production in the spleen, and attenuates inflammation in preclinical and clinical studies (Borovikova et al., 2000; Rosas-Ballina et al., 2008; Rosas-Ballina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borovikova et al., 2000 and Rosas-Ballina et al., 2008, 2011.

claim: Clinical VN stimulating devices are used in the treatment of epilepsy.
source: Clinical VN stimulating devices are used in the treatment of epilepsy (The Vagus Nerve Stimulation Study Group, 1995) and depression (Rush et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citation to The Vagus Nerve Stimulation Study Group, 1995.

claim: Clinical VN stimulating devices are used in the treatment of depression.
source: Clinical VN stimulating devices are used in the treatment of epilepsy (The Vagus Nerve Stimulation Study Group, 1995) and depression (Rush et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rush et al., 2000.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of tinnitus.
source: and are being studied in the treatment of brain disorders such as tinnitus (Tyler et al., 2017; Vanneste et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tyler et al., 2017 and Vanneste et al., 2017.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of stroke.
source: stroke (Engineer et al., 2019; Kimberley et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Engineer et al., 2019 and Kimberley et al., 2018.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
source: and Alzheimer's disease (Merrill et al., 2006; Sjögren et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Merrill et al., 2006 and Sjögren et al., 2002.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of heart failure.
source: as well as peripheral organ and systemic diseases, such as heart failure (De Ferrari et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Ferrari et al., 2017.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of cardiac arrhythmias.
source: cardiac arrhythmias (Huang et al., 2015; Nasi-Er et al., 2019; Stavrakis et al., 2015; Yamaguchi et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2015; Nasi-Er et al., 2019; Stavrakis et al., 2015; Yamaguchi et al., 2018.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of pulmonary hypertension.
source: pulmonary hypertension (Ntiloudi et al., 2019; Yoshida et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ntiloudi et al., 2019 and Yoshida et al., 2018.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.
source: rheumatoid arthritis (Koopman et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koopman et al., 2016.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of Crohn's disease.
source: Crohn's disease (Bonaz et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bonaz et al., 2016.

claim: VNS is being studied in the treatment of lupus.
source: and lupus (Aranow, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aranow, 2018.

claim: Additional possible indications for VNS include type 2 diabetes, obesity, and atherosclerosis.
source: Additional possible indications for vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) include common disorders in which inflammation is implicated, such as type 2 diabetes, obesity, and atherosclerosis (Couzin-Frankel, 2010; Furman et al., 2019; Slavich, 2015; Strowig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Couzin-Frankel, 2010; Furman et al., 2019; Slavich, 2015; Strowig et al., 2012.

claim: The majority of chronically implanted VN devices have been limited to neurological and cardiovascular diseases in rats, pigs, dogs, and other large animals.
source: to date the majority of chronically implanted VN devices have been limited to neurological and cardiovascular diseases in rats, pigs, dogs, and other large animals (Nasi-Er et al., 2019; Yamaguchi et al., 2018; Yoshida et al., 2018; Annoni et al., 2019; Beaumont et al., 2016; Chinda et al., 2016; Farrand et al., 2017; Li et al., 2004; Meyers et al., 2018; Nuntaphum et al., 2018; Yamakawa et al., 2015; Ganzer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work in large animal models.

claim: The mouse is currently the species of choice in the study of disease pathophysiology, genetic mechanisms, and drug screening.
source: The mouse is currently the species of choice in the study of disease pathophysiology, genetic mechanisms, and drug screening (Bryda, 2013; Perlman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bryda, 2013 and Perlman, 2016.

claim: VNS research in mice has been limited to acute stimulation.
source: However, VNS research in mice has been limited to acute stimulation (Bansal et al., 2012; Caravaca et al., 2019; de Lucas-Cerrillo et al., 2011; Huffman et al., 2019; Huston et al., 2006; Meneses et al., 2016; Saeed et al., 2005; Shukla et al., 2015; The et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior acute VNS studies in mice.

claim: Significant surgical and technical challenges accompany a mechanically and electrochemically stable long-term interface with the microscopic anatomy of the mouse VN.
source: primarily because of significant surgical and technical challenges that accompany a mechanically (Cuoco and Durand, 2000; Prasad et al., 2014; Rydevik et al., 1981) and electrochemically (McCreery et al., 1992; Negi et al., 2010) stable long-term interface with the microscopic anatomy of the mouse VN.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cuoco and Durand, 2000; Prasad et al., 2014; Rydevik et al., 1981; McCreery et al., 1992; Negi et al., 2010.

claim: The therapeutic role of VNS in chronic inflammatory diseases and the long-term effects on neural mechanisms are largely unexplored.
source: As a consequence, the therapeutic role of VNS in chronic inflammatory diseases and the long-term effects on neural mechanisms are largely unexplored.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of chronic VNS studies in mice as discussed in the introduction.

claim: A functional and reliable long-term VNS implant in the mouse is necessary to broaden the translational potential of VNS in chronic diseases.
source: A functional and reliable long-term VNS implant in the mouse is necessary to broaden the translational potential of VNS in chronic diseases and provides an experimental tool to probe the long-term effects of VN neuromodulation on autonomic and neuroimmune circuits.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the limitations of current models and the advantages of mouse models.

claim: The surgical technique was developed, refined, and validated through a collaboration between four research labs.
source: Here, we describe a surgical technique to permanently implant a micro-cuff electrode onto the mouse cervical vagus for long-term VNS—developed, refined, and validated through a collaboration between four research labs (two labs at Feinstein Institutes, University of Colorado, and New York University).
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the introduction.

claim: The implant produced a standardized, long-lasting, functionally consistent implant with expected stimulus-elicited physiological responses that persist for at least 4 weeks.
source: This produced a standardized, long-lasting, functionally consistent implant with expected stimulus-elicited physiological responses that persist for at least 4 weeks.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal data in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: The implant does not interfere with physiological VN-mediated reflexes, including baroreflex, lung stretch reflex, and feeding reflexes.
source: Because the implant does not interfere with physiological VN-mediated reflexes, including baroreflex, lung stretch reflex, and feeding reflexes
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The implant successfully inhibits serum TNF levels in acute endotoxemia.
source: and successfully inhibits serum TNF levels in acute endotoxemia
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: 150 μm MicroLeads cuff electrodes and 100 μm CorTec microsling cuffs were commercially fabricated and used for cuff preparation.
source: 150 μm MicroLeads cuff electrodes (MicroLeads Neuro, Gaithersburg, MD) and 100 μm CorTec microsling cuffs (CorTec, Freiburg, Germany) were commercially fabricated and used for cuff preparation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the methods and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MicroLeads cuffs are constructed with medical-grade assembly techniques using biocompatible materials, largely silicone, polyimide, and platinum iridium.
source: MicroLeads cuffs are constructed with medical-grade assembly techniques using biocompatible materials, largely silicone, polyimide, and platinum iridium, and utilize a self-closing mechanism.
evidence: This is a description of the electrode materials provided in the methods.

claim: MicroLeads cuffs utilize a self-closing mechanism.
source: MicroLeads cuffs are constructed with medical-grade assembly techniques using biocompatible materials, largely silicone, polyimide, and platinum iridium, and utilize a self-closing mechanism.
evidence: This is a description of the electrode mechanism provided in the methods.

claim: CorTec microsling cuffs are constructed with biocompatible materials including a silicone base, platinum iridium contacts, and a parylene C coating.
source: CorTec microsling cuffs are also constructed with biocompatible materials including a silicone base, platinum iridium contacts, and a parylene C coating, and utilize a buckle-like closing mechanism.
evidence: This is a description of the electrode materials provided in the methods.

claim: CorTec microsling cuffs utilize a buckle-like closing mechanism.
source: CorTec microsling cuffs are also constructed with biocompatible materials including a silicone base, platinum iridium contacts, and a parylene C coating, and utilize a buckle-like closing mechanism.
evidence: This is a description of the electrode mechanism provided in the methods.

claim: Bipolar platinum-iridium micro-cuff electrodes were soldered to gold sockets after cutting the lead wires to a length of 2.5–3.0 cm.
source: These bipolar platinum-iridium micro-cuff electrodes were soldered to gold sockets after cutting the lead wires to a length of 2.5–3.0 cm (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the methods and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Electrical impedance was measured in saline for each electrode at 1 kHz using MicroProbes Impedance Tester.
source: Electrical impedance was measured in saline for each electrode at 1 kHz using MicroProbes Impedance Tester (MicroProbes, Gaithersburg, MD).
evidence: This is a methodological detail provided in the methods section.

claim: Male C57BL/6 mice were purchased from Charles River Laboratories at the age of 8–12 weeks.
source: Male C57BL/6 mice were purchased from Charles River Laboratories (Wilmington, MA) at the age of 8–12 weeks.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Animals were housed under 12 hr light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water.
source: Animals were housed under 12 hr light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: All animal experiments complied with relevant ethical guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research and University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus.
source: All animal experiments complied with relevant ethical guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research (protocol numbers: 2016-029, 2017-010, and 2019-010) and University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (protocol number: 00238).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: VNS produces decreases in HR as well as changes in BR.
source: VNS produces decreases in HR as well as changes in BR (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by physiological traces shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The magnitude of HR reduction is dependent on current intensity.
source: The magnitude of HR reduction is dependent on current intensity (r = 0.8971, p=0.0062) (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: BR shows more variable responses to VNS, including slowing down and acceleration of breathing.
source: whereas BR shows more variable responses, including slowing down and acceleration of breathing (Figure 2A, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by physiological traces shown in Figures 2A and 3A.

claim: In conscious mice, VNS produces comparable dose-dependent HR responses.
source: In conscious mice (n = 2), VNS produces comparable dose-dependent HR responses (Video 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Video 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Animals receiving awake VNS do not show any signs of distress or visible changes in BR.
source: Animals receiving awake VNS do not show any signs of distress or visible changes in BR.
evidence: This is an observational finding reported in the results.

claim: HRT is defined as the minimum current intensity required to elicit an ~5–15% reduction in HR using a stimulus train of 300 bi-phasic, charge-balanced, square pulses at a pulsing frequency of 30 Hz.
source: HRT was defined as the minimum current intensity required to elicit an ~5–15% reduction in HR using a stimulus train of 300 bi-phasic, charge-balanced, square pulses at a pulsing frequency of 30 Hz with short (100 μs) or long (500–1000 μs) pulse widths (PWs).
evidence: This is a methodological definition provided in the methods section.

claim: VNS delivered using the implant elicits drops in HR and changes in breathing for up to 8 weeks post-implantation.
source: VNS delivered using the implant elicits drops in HR and changes in breathing for up to 8 weeks post-implantation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Initial HRT values determined with short PW were variable among animals (range = 30–400 μA, mean = 156, SD = 118, n = 20 mice).
source: Initial HRT values determined with short PW were variable among animals (range = 30–400 μA, mean = 156, SD = 118, n = 20 mice)
evidence: This is a statistical summary of experimental data.

claim: Initial HRT values increased over the first week post-implantation.
source: and increased over the first week post-implantation (Pearson r = 0.89, p = 0.0064, n = 20 mice) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HRT values determined with long PWs did not change significantly with time.
source: whereas HRT values determined with long PWs did not change significantly with time (r = −0.22, p NS, n = 26 mice) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HRT values with short PW were 54% greater on average than those with long PW.
source: HRT values with short PW were 54% greater on average than those with long PW, and that relationship was maintained over time (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pre-implantation impedance values did not correlate with initial HRT.
source: Pre-implantation impedance values did not correlate with initial HRT (r = 0.34, p NS, n = 15 mice) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bipolar electrical impedance did not increase over the period of testing.
source: and bipolar electrical impedance did not increase over the period of testing (r = −0.68, p = 0.0415, n = 29) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was no correlation between changes in electrical impedance and HRT values.
source: Interestingly, there was no correlation between changes in electrical impedance and HRT values (r = 0.05, p NS)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: In some mice, nonfunctional cuffs continued to have relatively low impedance values despite their inability to induce a physiological response.
source: in some mice, nonfunctional cuffs continued to have relatively low impedance values despite their inability to induce a physiological response (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Percentage of mice with functional implants at 4 weeks post-implantation increased from 40% in cohort 1 to 90% in cohort 3.
source: Implant failure occurred more frequently in earlier compared to later cohorts: percentage of mice with functional implants at 4 weeks post-implantation increased from 40% in cohort 1 to 90% in cohort 3 (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: In a separate group of animals, implants were 96% functional during the first 5 days after surgery (50/52 mice, excluding deaths during surgery).
source: In a separate group of animals, implants were 96% functional during the first 5 days after surgery (50/52 mice, excluding deaths during surgery)
evidence: This is a statistical summary of experimental data.

claim: Functional implants tested again in days 6–14 had a success rate of 76% (38/50).
source: functional implants were tested again in days 6–14, with a success rate of 76% (38/50) (Table 1 and Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3F.

claim: In a random subset of implants, 17/18 and 11/13 were functional in the 15–30 and 30+ days period, respectively.
source: In a random subset of those implants, 17/18 and 11/13 were functional in the 15–30 and 30+ days period, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Electrode failures occurred during the first 2 weeks post-implantation and implant functionality stabilized thereafter.
source: Overall, electrode failures occurred during the first 2 weeks post-implantation and implant functionality stabilized thereafter (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Table 1.

claim: The change in body weight of implanted animals during the first and second weeks post-implantation is not different than sham surgery controls.
source: The change in body weight of implanted animals during the first and second weeks post-implantation is not different than sham surgery controls (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The average food intake during the first 2 weeks is similar in implanted and sham surgery groups.
source: Further, the average food intake during the first 2 weeks is similar in both groups (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The average food intake in implanted and sham surgery groups is within the range of reported daily average intake in healthy animals.
source: and within the range of reported daily average intake in healthy animals (Bachmanov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to published data cited from Bachmanov et al., 2002.

claim: Implanted mice do not exhibit elevated levels of serum TNF 2–3 weeks post-implantation.
source: Implanted mice do not exhibit elevated levels of serum TNF 2–3 weeks post-implantation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both implanted and naive animals have similar HR at baseline.
source: Both implanted and naive animals have similar HR at baseline, with a similarly significant decrease upon phenylephrine injection (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Both implanted and naive animals show a similarly significant decrease in HR upon phenylephrine injection.
source: Both implanted and naive animals have similar HR at baseline, with a similarly significant decrease upon phenylephrine injection (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The baroreflex sensitivity index is not significantly different between implanted and naive groups.
source: Further, the baroreflex sensitivity index, expressed as the ratio of heart rate change (ΔHR) to systolic blood pressure change (ΔSBP), is not significantly different between the two groups (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mice with long-term implants exhibit changes in breathing similar to those induced in acute VNS experiments.
source: We found that mice with long-term implants exhibit changes in breathing (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) similar to those induced in acute VNS experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mice with 9- to 17-day-old implants that received three VNS doses showed significantly decreased serum TNF compared to sham stimulation.
source: We found that VNS significantly decreases serum TNF in stimulated animals compared to sham stimulation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VNS parameters of 1 mA intensity, 250 μs PW, 30 Hz frequency, 5 min duration did not usually induce a change in HR during stimulation.
source: Notably, these parameters did not usually induce a change in HR during stimulation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: One-time VNS does not produce a significant decrease in TNF levels overall.
source: Overall, we found that one-time VNS does not produce a significant decrease in TNF levels.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results from the one-time VNS experiment.

claim: Out of 14 stimulated mice in the one-time VNS experiment, VNS produced a decrease in HR in seven animals.
source: However, out of the 14 stimulated mice, VNS produced a decrease in HR in seven animals, of which four exhibited more than ~40% decrease in serum TNF compared to sham-stimulated controls and animals with no HR response (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Four out of seven animals with HR response to VNS exhibited more than ~40% decrease in serum TNF compared to sham-stimulated controls and animals with no HR response.
source: However, out of the 14 stimulated mice, VNS produced a decrease in HR in seven animals, of which four exhibited more than ~40% decrease in serum TNF compared to sham-stimulated controls and animals with no HR response (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mice that lacked a physiological response to VNS had TNF levels comparable to sham-stimulated controls.
source: Mice that lacked a physiological response had TNF levels comparable to sham-stimulated controls.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The implant site appeared healed and exhibited moderate tissue growth encompassing the lead wires and cuff surfaces in animals with both functional and nonfunctional implants.
source: The implant site appeared healed and exhibited moderate tissue growth encompassing the lead wires and cuff surfaces in animals with both functional and nonfunctional implants (example from 12 days post-implantation shown in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation supported by images shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Histological analysis of explanted cuffed left nerves revealed preserved nerve fibers compared with non-cuffed left nerves from naive controls with no obvious axonal pathology or inflammation.
source: Histological analysis of explanted cuffed left nerves revealed preserved nerve fibers compared with non-cuffed left nerves from naive controls with no obvious axonal pathology or inflammation (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The explanted nerves were surrounded by increased amounts of fibrotic tissue.
source: The explanted nerves were surrounded by increased amounts of fibrotic tissue (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The explanted nerves exhibited thickened perineurium.
source: or exhibited thickened perineurium (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In animals examined 6 weeks post-implantation, histological analysis of cross-sections of whole neck blocks just above the cuff margin revealed similar preserved nerves.
source: In another group of animals (n = 6) in which we examined cross-sections of whole neck blocks just above the cuff margin 6 weeks post-implantation, histological analysis revealed similar preserved nerves (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: VNS causes reduction in HR mainly through activation of efferent cardioinhibitory fibers.
source: VNS causes reduction in HR, mainly through activation of efferent cardioinhibitory fibers (Buschman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buschman et al., 2006.

claim: In a functional neural interface, increasing stimulation intensity leads to recruitment of more fibers, and hence a larger stimulus-evoked response.
source: In a functional neural interface, increasing stimulation intensity leads to recruitment of more fibers, and hence a larger stimulus-evoked response (Chang et al., 2020; Zaaimi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2020 and Zaaimi et al., 2008.

claim: Higher stimulation intensities lead to the ordered recruitment of different fiber types according to size: from large A, to intermediate-size B, to small C fibers.
source: Additionally, higher stimulation intensities lead to the ordered recruitment of different fiber types according to size: from large A, to intermediate-size B, to small C fibers (Blair and Erlanger, 1933).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blair and Erlanger, 1933.

claim: The variable changes in BR observed at different stimulation intensities can be explained by activation of either A or C fibers, which differentially affect breathing in mice and rats.
source: The variable changes in BR we observed at different stimulation intensities (Figure 2A, Figure 3A) can be explained by activation of either A or C fibers, which differentially affect breathing in mice (Chang et al., 2015) and in rats (Chang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Chang et al., 2015 and Chang et al., 2020, and data shown in Figures 2A and 3A.

claim: A functional nerve interface exhibits a characteristic relationship between intensity and PW (strength-duration): to produce a response, lower stimulation intensities are required at longer PWs, and vice versa.
source: In addition, a functional nerve interface exhibits a characteristic relationship between intensity and PW (strength-duration): to produce a response, lower stimulation intensities are required at longer PWs, and vice versa (Geddes and Bourland, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geddes and Bourland, 1985.

claim: The long-term implants produced HR responses at lower intensities with longer PWs, a relationship that remains consistent with time.
source: Our long-term implants produced HR responses at lower intensities with longer PWs, a relationship that remains consistent with time (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The variability in baseline thresholds at the time of implantation is not explained by differences in pre-implantation impedance and is likely due to variability in electrode placement, which affects fiber engagement.
source: The variability in baseline thresholds at the time of implantation is not explained by differences in pre-implantation impedance and is likely due to variability in electrode placement, which affects fiber engagement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between pre-implantation impedance and initial HRT.

claim: The gradual increase in HRT over time can be attributed to fibrotic encapsulation of electrode surfaces, a process that evolves over days to weeks.
source: The gradual increase in HRT over time can be attributed to fibrotic encapsulation of electrode surfaces, a process that evolves over days to weeks and is known to reduce the efficacy of implanted neural interfaces by increasing tissue resistivity and the distance between the nerve and the electrode contact surface (Anderson et al., 2008; Grill and Mortimer, 1994; Farah et al., 2019; Vasudevan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2008; Grill and Mortimer, 1994; Farah et al., 2019; Vasudevan et al., 2017.

claim: Fibrotic encapsulation is known to reduce the efficacy of implanted neural interfaces by increasing tissue resistivity and the distance between the nerve and the electrode contact surface.
source: a process that evolves over days to weeks and is known to reduce the efficacy of implanted neural interfaces by increasing tissue resistivity and the distance between the nerve and the electrode contact surface (Anderson et al., 2008; Grill and Mortimer, 1994; Farah et al., 2019; Vasudevan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2008; Grill and Mortimer, 1994; Farah et al., 2019; Vasudevan et al., 2017.

claim: Increased tissue growth within the cuff comprised fibrotic tissue around the nerve.
source: We observed increased tissue growth within the cuff, which, upon histological examination, comprised fibrotic tissue around the nerve (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Longer PWs were more effective in eliciting HRT in aged implants because the effect of distance on activation threshold is weaker for long pulses than for short pulses.
source: This may explain why longer PWs were more effective in eliciting HRT in aged implants: the effect of distance on activation threshold is weaker for long pulses than for short pulses (Grill and Mortimer, 1995).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Grill and Mortimer, 1995.

claim: Since animals exhibit variable threshold values at baseline and across time, employing fixed parameters would result in variable fiber recruitment, inconsistent therapeutic dosing, and possibly undesirable off-target effects.
source: Since animals exhibit variable threshold values at baseline and across time, employing fixed parameters would result in variable fiber recruitment, inconsistent therapeutic dosing, and, possibly, undesirable off-target effects.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observed variability in HRT.

claim: Previous reports from rat and large animal models implemented a similar approach to adjust stimulation intensity using respiratory twitching and HR to standardize stimulation protocols, but not on a dose-by-dose basis.
source: Previous reports from rat and large animal models implemented a similar approach to adjust stimulation intensity using respiratory twitching (Yoshida et al., 2018; Nishizaki et al., 2016), and HR (Huffman et al., 2019; Chapleau et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2014) to standardize stimulation protocols, but not on a dose-by-dose basis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2018; Nishizaki et al., 2016; Huffman et al., 2019; Chapleau et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2014.

claim: Electrical impedance is commonly used as a measure of electrode integrity and performance.
source: Notably, electrical impedance, which is commonly used as a measure of electrode integrity and performance (Straka et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Straka et al., 2018.

claim: Electrical impedance did not always correlate with changes in HRT on an individual implant basis as implants aged.
source: Notably, electrical impedance, which is commonly used as a measure of electrode integrity and performance (Straka et al., 2018), did not always correlate with changes in HRT on an individual implant basis as implants aged (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Impedance tended to decrease over the period of implantation as HRT increased.
source: In fact, impedance tended to decrease over the period of implantation as HRT increased (Figure 3B, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: Three cases of lead wire breakage occurred out of nine nonfunctional implants in three groups of animals.
source: We observed three cases of lead wire breakage out of nine nonfunctional implants in three groups of animals.
evidence: This is a summary of observed failures.

claim: In all three cases of lead wire breakage, breakage occurred at the junction between the lead wire and electrode, exposing a mechanically weak point that should be reinforced during manufacturing.
source: In all three cases, breakage occurred at the junction between the lead wire and electrode, exposing a mechanically weak point that should be reinforced during manufacturing.
evidence: This is an observation and recommendation based on the failure analysis.

claim: Neural electrodes can degrade with long-term use.
source: Neural electrodes can degrade with long-term use (Negi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Negi et al., 2010.

claim: Electrode degradation is accelerated at stimulation intensities that exceed the electrode's ability to transfer charge without undergoing irreversible damage (CIC).
source: This process is accelerated at stimulation intensities that exceed the electrode's ability to transfer charge without undergoing irreversible damage (CIC) (Negi et al., 2010; Merrill et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Negi et al., 2010 and Merrill et al., 2005.

claim: The damage imparted by exceeding CIC is not limited to the electrode but can affect the nerve as well.
source: The damage imparted by exceeding this threshold is not limited to the electrode but can affect the nerve as well (Cogan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cogan et al., 2016.

claim: ICIC was not exceeded in most animals.
source: Although we did not examine explanted electrodes for morphological or electrochemical changes, we did take note of platinum-iridium's maximum charge capacity (Cogan, 2008), which was not exceeded in most animals (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: On the few occasions when ICIC was exceeded, it likely did not cause significant damage to the electrode as the stimulation events were brief (10 s) and limited in number.
source: On the few occasions when ICIC was exceeded, it likely did not cause significant damage to the electrode as the stimulation events were brief (10 s) and limited in number.
evidence: This is an inference based on the brief duration and limited number of stimulation events.

claim: Mechanical forces generated by chronic cuffing can damage nerves.
source: Mechanical forces generated by chronic cuffing can also damage nerves (Agnew and McCreery, 1990; Larsen et al., 1998; Somann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Agnew and McCreery, 1990; Larsen et al., 1998; Somann et al., 2018.

claim: Histological analysis revealed viable nerve tissue with no obvious fiber loss or axonal fragmentation.
source: Our histological analysis revealed viable nerve tissue with no obvious fiber loss or axonal fragmentation.
evidence: This is supported by histological data presented in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Damage to the nerve is unlikely to be a contributing factor to increased HRT over time.
source: Therefore, damage to the nerve is unlikely to be a contributing factor to increased HRT over time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the histological findings.

claim: Surgical proficiency contributed greatly to implant success.
source: Apart from electrode- and tissue-related factors, we found that surgical proficiency contributed greatly to implant success, which is evident from the increase in successful implantations over successive groups of animals (Table 1, cohorts 1–3, from earlier to later) completed over several months by an initially inexperienced surgeon.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Chronic cuffing of the vagus could, in principle, cause damage to the nerve, thereby affecting functions such as appetite, respiration, and BP.
source: Chronic cuffing of the vagus could, in principle, cause damage to the nerve, thereby affecting these functions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential risks.

claim: Severing the VN causes weight loss in mice.
source: For example, severing the VN causes weight loss in mice (Kral and Görtz, 1981)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kral and Görtz, 1981.

claim: Severing the VN affects appetite and gastric transit times among other factors.
source: by affecting appetite and gastric transit times among other factors (Dezfuli et al., 2018; Khound et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dezfuli et al., 2018 and Khound et al., 2017.

claim: The VN mediates the afferent and the efferent-parasympathetic component of the baroreflex.
source: The VN also mediates the afferent and the efferent-parasympathetic component of the baroreflex, a homeostatic mechanism that maintains BP within normal range by modulating HR (Glick and Braunwald, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glick and Braunwald, 1965.

claim: The baroreflex is a homeostatic mechanism that maintains BP within normal range by modulating HR.
source: The VN also mediates the afferent and the efferent-parasympathetic component of the baroreflex, a homeostatic mechanism that maintains BP within normal range by modulating HR (Glick and Braunwald, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glick and Braunwald, 1965.

claim: In an intact system, an increase in BP causes a reflexive decrease in HR by increasing vagal activity.
source: In an intact system, an increase in BP causes a reflexive decrease in HR by increasing vagal activity, which is consistent with our observations in implanted animals.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge consistent with the experimental observations.

claim: The vagus carries vital sensory information from the lung to regulate breathing.
source: The vagus also carries vital sensory information from the lung to regulate breathing (Carr and Undem, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carr and Undem, 2003.

claim: Vagal sensory information from the lung is mediated by large, myelinated A fibers that cause slowing down of breathing and small, unmyelinated C fibers that cause rapid shallow breathing.
source: Recent evidence has shown that this is mediated by large, myelinated A fibers that cause slowing down of breathing and small, unmyelinated C fibers that cause rapid shallow breathing (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2015.

claim: Vagal sensory pathways control respiration by reflexive activity that changes BR, such as the Herring–Breuer inflation and deflation reflexes.
source: These sensory pathways control respiration by reflexive activity that changes BR, such as the Herring–Breuer inflation and deflation reflexes (Schelegle and Green, 2001; Siniaia et al., 2000; Yu, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schelegle and Green, 2001; Siniaia et al., 2000; Yu, 2016.

claim: Patients receiving VNS for epilepsy do not show changes in tidal volume or BR during wakefulness.
source: Patients receiving VNS for epilepsy do not show changes in tidal volume or BR during wakefulness (Banzett et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banzett et al., 1999.

claim: Patients receiving VNS for epilepsy exhibit decreases in air flow when VNS is activated during sleep.
source: yet exhibit decreases in air flow when VNS is activated during sleep (Murray et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murray et al., 2001.

claim: The preserved reflexes in implanted animals are mediated by large, myelinated fibers.
source: Importantly, the fact that these preserved reflexes are mediated by large, myelinated fibers further supports the viability of the nerve after chronic cuffing as large fibers are the most sensitive to chronic compression injury (Dahlin et al., 1989).
evidence: This is an inference based on the preserved reflexes and citation to Dahlin et al., 1989.

claim: Large fibers are the most sensitive to chronic compression injury.
source: as large fibers are the most sensitive to chronic compression injury (Dahlin et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dahlin et al., 1989.

claim: The potential wide therapeutic applicability of VNS lies in part in its ability to modulate inflammation.
source: The potential wide therapeutic applicability of VNS lies in part in its ability to modulate inflammation, a process fundamental to the pathogenesis of many diseases (Couzin-Frankel, 2010; Furman et al., 2019; Slavich, 2015; Strowig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Couzin-Frankel, 2010; Furman et al., 2019; Slavich, 2015; Strowig et al., 2012.

claim: Inflammation is a process fundamental to the pathogenesis of many diseases.
source: a process fundamental to the pathogenesis of many diseases (Couzin-Frankel, 2010; Furman et al., 2019; Slavich, 2015; Strowig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Couzin-Frankel, 2010; Furman et al., 2019; Slavich, 2015; Strowig et al., 2012.

claim: VNS controls inflammation by activating the inflammatory reflex, defined as an afferent arm that responds to inflammation in the periphery via vagal sensory neurons and an efferent arm that suppresses activation of macrophages via vagal motor neurons that project to the spleen.
source: VNS controls inflammation by activating the IR, defined as an afferent arm that responds to inflammation in the periphery via vagal sensory neurons and an efferent arm that suppresses activation of macrophages via vagal motor neurons that project to the spleen (Tracey, 2009; Tracey, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tracey, 2009 and Tracey, 2002.

claim: The anti-inflammatory effect of VNS was first described in a model of LPS endotoxemia, wherein acute VNS suppressed TNF release.
source: This effect was first described in a model of LPS endotoxemia, wherein acute VNS suppressed TNF release (Borovikova et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borovikova et al., 2000.

claim: TNF suppression in LPS endotoxemia has been established as a standard functional read-out of the anti-inflammatory effects of VNS.
source: and has since been established as a standard functional read-out of the anti-inflammatory effects of VNS (Caravaca et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Caravaca et al., 2019.

claim: Chronic cuffing of the VN might suppress efferent signaling that could reduce the anti-inflammatory actions of VNS due to loss of nerve fibers smaller than what could be detected histologically.
source: Chronic cuffing of the VN might suppress efferent signaling that could reduce the anti-inflammatory actions of VNS (Somann et al., 2018) due to loss of nerve fibers smaller than what we could detect histologically (Nitz et al., 1986; Szabo and Sharkey, 1993).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to Somann et al., 2018; Nitz et al., 1986; Szabo and Sharkey, 1993.

claim: Some animals in the single-dose group could be non-responders, a common occurrence in these studies.
source: Alternatively, some animals in the single-dose group could be non-responders, a common occurrence in these studies (Caravaca et al., 2019; Huffman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caravaca et al., 2019 and Huffman et al., 2019.

claim: A HR response does not necessarily mean engagement of the inflammatory reflex.
source: Our data indicate that a HR response does not necessarily mean engagement of the IR, consistent with previous findings in acute studies (Huffman et al., 2019; Huston et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to Huffman et al., 2019 and Huston et al., 2007.

claim: Vagal cholinergic fibers signaling to the spleen via abdominal sympathetic ganglia to suppress inflammation may lie in distinct parts of the nerve from those innervating the heart to cause drops in HR.
source: Anatomically, vagal cholinergic fibers signaling to the spleen via abdominal sympathetic ganglia to suppress inflammation (Kressel et al., 2020) may lie in distinct parts of the nerve from those innervating the heart to cause drops in HR (Rajendran et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Kressel et al., 2020 and Rajendran et al., 2019.

claim: It is unknown if the inflammatory reflex is activated by engagement of efferent fibers, or additionally by afferent fibers.
source: It is unknown if the IR is activated by engagement of efferent fibers, or additionally by afferent fibers, some of which are activated by lower VNS intensities.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Recent reports implicate both afferent and efferent pathways in the anti-inflammatory actions of VNS.
source: Recent reports implicate both afferent and efferent pathways (Kressel et al., 2020; Murray et al., 2021; Olofsson et al., 2015) in the anti-inflammatory actions of VNS
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kressel et al., 2020; Murray et al., 2021; Olofsson et al., 2015.

claim: In a study by Huffman et al., 2019, TNF was suppressed using 90% of HRT, without reduction in HR.
source: and in a study by Huffman et al., 2019, TNF was suppressed using 90% of HRT, without reduction in HR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huffman et al., 2019.

claim: Stimulating at or above HRT could activate compensatory reflexes that might alter the anti-inflammatory effect of VNS.
source: Moreover, stimulating at or above HRT could activate compensatory reflexes that might alter the anti-inflammatory effect of VNS, as shown in one report where stimulation at higher frequencies and amplitudes resulted in an increase in TNF in healthy animals (Tsaava et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Tsaava et al., 2020.

claim: Stimulation at higher frequencies and amplitudes resulted in an increase in TNF in healthy animals.
source: as shown in one report where stimulation at higher frequencies and amplitudes resulted in an increase in TNF in healthy animals (Tsaava et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsaava et al., 2020.

claim: HRT is a practical method to estimate stimulation dose required to achieve consistent efferent, parasympathetic fiber recruitment in an implant.
source: We suggest using HRT as a practical method to estimate stimulation dose required to achieve consistent efferent, parasympathetic fiber recruitment in an implant, thereby reducing variability related to the nerve anatomy itself and the nerve-electrode interface.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Stimulus intensities required to engage specific circuits and organs could be determined experimentally relative to HRT.
source: Stimulus intensities required to engage specific circuits and organs could then be determined experimentally relative to HRT (Huffman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a recommendation supported by citation to Huffman et al., 2019.

claim: A fixed set of parameters could be used in recovered animals beyond the first week when the procedure is optimized and variability minimized.
source: A fixed set of parameters could still be used in recovered animals beyond the first week when the procedure is optimized, and variability minimized, as we show in the endotoxemia experiment with multiple doses (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: The shorter PW of 250 μs could explain why 1 mA did not usually result in HR changes in the multiple-dose endotoxemia experiment.
source: In this experiment, animals received VNS with 250 μs PW, compared with the 500 μs PW used in other validation cohorts. This shorter PW could explain why 1 mA did not usually result in HR changes (Figure 5C), as HRT is generally greater for shorter PWs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between PW and HRT shown in Figure 3C.

claim: This report is the first demonstration of chronic VNS in the mouse that provides longitudinal evidence of stimulus-elicited physiological responses.
source: To our knowledge, this report is the first demonstration of chronic VNS in the mouse that provides longitudinal evidence of stimulus-elicited physiological responses.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The cervical VN comprises parasympathetic motor and visceral sensory fibers that regulate many physiological functions including HR and breathing.
source: The cervical VN comprises parasympathetic motor and visceral sensory fibers that regulate many physiological functions including HR and breathing (Berthoud and Neuhuber, 2000; Agostoni et al., 1957; Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berthoud and Neuhuber, 2000; Agostoni et al., 1957; Chang et al., 2015.
